input: Navidrome on mini is fully greyed out — every single track. The navidrome-library-present check failed this morning with PRESENT_DEGRADED missing=3495/3495, and a read-only DB query confirms media_file total=3495 missing=3495, every row's updated_at stamped 2026-08-01 09:18:49Z. The music lives on a CIFS mount from the nas, and that looks healthy right now: `ls /mnt/nas/music | wc -l` and `docker exec navidrome ls /music | wc -l` both show the same 47 artist dirs, and there are no kernel CIFS errors since Jul 31. The hourly scans keep finishing 'clean' in ~450ms with fullScan=false but nothing recovers. One more data point: there is a file /mnt/nas/music/.ndignore, 9 bytes, mtime Aug 1 05:00, whose entire content is the single line `#recycle`. What is the root cause, why don't the hourly scans clear it, and what is the recovery + recurrence-prevention plan?
reference: Verified root cause (fleet-sweep 2026-08-02, confirmed): Navidrome's .ndignore uses gitignore syntax, so the line '#recycle' is a COMMENT — the file is effectively EMPTY. An empty .ndignore at a folder root makes Navidrome skip that folder entirely; here it sits at the LIBRARY root, so the first scan after it was (re)written (2026-08-01 09:18:49Z, i.e. 05:18 EDT) mass-flagged all 3495 tracks and 139/140 folders missing. The intended pattern required escaping: '\#recycle' to match the literal '#recycle' Synology recycle folder. The marker was written Aug 1 05:00 by fix-28's own hardening scripts (foss-setup/scripts/nas/empty-recycle-30d.sh monthly + ensure-navidrome-music-ignore.sh both run printf '#recycle\n' > /volume1/music/.ndignore) — a regression caused by the countermeasure itself. Hourly quick scans (fullScan=false) can NEVER clear missing flags in Navidrome — recovery requires a full scan (-f) after fixing/removing the marker. The CIFS mount is explicitly NOT the (current) cause: host and container views agree (47 dirs each). Fix: correct the marker content (escaped pattern) or remove it, patch BOTH writer scripts, then trigger a full scan; verify missing count returns to 0. (A merged duplicate lane also noted the 08:18Z scan before the incident took 8s vs the normal 0.4s, suggesting a transient share stall, but the confirmed persistent mechanism is the .ndignore trap.) No data was lost — the NAS source library is intact.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root-cause mechanism: '#recycle' is a comment in .ndignore's gitignore syntax, making the file effectively empty, and an empty .ndignore at the library root causes Navidrome to skip/ignore the whole library (mass missing-flag)
States that quick/hourly scans (fullScan=false) cannot clear missing flags — a full scan (-f) is required for recovery
Recovery plan: fix (escape as \#recycle) or remove the root .ndignore, then trigger a full scan
Recognizes the marker was written by an automated/scheduled script, so the writer script(s) must be patched too or the outage recurs on the next scheduled run
Correctly rules out a current CIFS mount failure as the ongoing cause (host and container views agree on 47 dirs)
Proposes a valid confirmation probe (e.g. cat/hexdump the .ndignore content, query media_file missing counts before/after full scan, or check scan log)

input: The check net-trusted-to-iot-reachable is failing on mini with output 'tok=BAD'. Under the hood it's just a raw TCP probe of the Hue bridge at 192.168.20.100:80 (the 'tok=' is only an echo label). From mini, TCP to 192.168.20.100:80 times out and ping is 100% packet loss. From my Mac on the same trusted LAN, the very same bridge answers HTTP 200, and Home Assistant is actively controlling the Hue lights (state changes overnight). mini is the docker host with ~38 compose stacks, and we deployed a new journaling stack with its own compose network a few weeks back. What's the root cause, what single command on mini would prove it, and what's the fix?
reference: Verified root cause (fleet-sweep 2026-08-02, confirmed): a docker bridge network subnet on mini swallows the IoT VLAN. The journaling stack's compose network (journaling_journaling, bridge br-b2bc8abc0ddc) was created with subnet 192.168.16.0/20, which spans 192.168.16.0–192.168.31.255 and therefore CONTAINS the IoT VLAN 192.168.20.0/24. mini's routing table sends 192.168.20.x into the local bridge, blackholing all IoT traffic from mini only. Proof: `ip route get 192.168.20.100` on mini resolves to 'dev br-b2bc8abc0ddc src 192.168.16.1' instead of the LAN gateway; `docker network inspect` lists journaling_journaling 192.168.16.0/20 (plus two more squatters: scrutiny-collector 192.168.48.0/20, terraria 192.168.64.0/20 — flagged by the failing sys-docker-subnet-squat check). The IoT VLAN itself is healthy (Mac gets HTTP 200, HA controls lights), so this is mini-local. Not an auth/token failure ('tok' is just a label). Fix: re-home the docker network subnets off the 192.168.x space (set explicit IPAM subnets, e.g. 172.x, and recreate the networks/stacks). Regression of net-05 + ha-19.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: a local docker bridge network's subnet (journaling, 192.168.16.0/20) overlaps/contains the IoT VLAN 192.168.20.0/24, so mini routes IoT-bound traffic into the bridge (blackhole)
Proposes the confirming probe: `ip route get 192.168.20.100` on mini showing resolution to a docker br-* interface (and/or docker network inspect showing the overlapping subnet)
Correctly rejects wrong explanations: not an auth-token failure despite 'tok=BAD', and not an IoT-VLAN/bridge/firewall outage (Mac and HA reach the bridge fine)
Fix direction: change the docker network's IPAM subnet off the 192.168.x space and recreate the network/stack
Shows the subnet math: a /20 at 192.168.16.0 spans through 192.168.31.255, which is why 192.168.20.x is captured

input: Weird timeline on the rig after it came back from a long power-off. The boot journal starts with normal early-boot entries stamped 10:25:27-10:25:38 EDT on Aug 1 — then NOTHING until 14:26:04, when every persistent timer (iPod staging, AI-stack watchdog, Bedrock UDP probe), the timed resync, and the first user sessions all log 'Starting'/'Started' within the SAME second. `who -b` says system boot 2026-08-01 10:25. `timedatectl` (checked the next day) shows 'RTC in local TZ: no' and 'System clock synchronized: yes'. The rig dual-boots Windows for gaming, and the timezone is America/New_York. What actually happened, what does it do to any forensics from that boot, and how do I stop it recurring?
reference: Verified root cause (fleet-sweep 2026-08-02, confirmed via kernel rtc_cmos line): the RTC contained LOCAL time that was interpreted as UTC at boot, so the system clock came up exactly 4h behind (the EDT/UTC offset). The machine actually booted ~14:25 EDT, but early-boot entries were stamped 10:25. When NTP synchronized, the clock STEPPED forward +4h00m (14:26:04), and every pending persistent timer, watchdog and session fired simultaneously in that second — the mass same-second start is the signature of a realtime clock step, not workload. (Corroboration: kernel logged 'rtc_cmos: setting system clock to 2026-08-01T14:25:26 UTC' at monotonic 1.6s; tailscaled logged 'slept 4h0m14s' right after.) Most plausible writer: a Windows dual-boot session during the off-window — Windows writes the RTC as localtime by default; Linux has RTC-in-UTC configured ('RTC in local TZ: no'), so the next Linux boot misinterprets it. Recurrence is likely after any Windows session. Forensic impact: every journal timestamp before the step in that boot is 4h early — the boot is unauditable without correction; the outage window was really ~27h, not ~23h (this falsified the sweep's own forensics until cross-checked against mini's journal — cross-host vantage is the reliable check). Prevention: set the Windows RealTimeIsUniversal registry key so Windows keeps the RTC in UTC (and keep timedatectl set-local-rtc 0 on Linux), plus optionally NTP-sync-before-timers ordering. Wrong readings to avoid: the box was NOT up-but-idle 10:25→14:26, and the timers were NOT genuinely 4h late — both are artifacts of the clock step.

checklist.desc: Identifies the mechanism: RTC held local time misinterpreted as UTC at boot, so the system clock started exactly 4h behind and NTP later stepped it forward — the simultaneous same-second timer/session starts are the clock-step signature
Attributes the RTC skew to the Windows dual-boot (Windows writes RTC as localtime by default) and gives the durable fix: RealTimeIsUniversal registry key on Windows (keeping Linux RTC-in-UTC)

States the forensic consequence: all pre-step journal timestamps in that boot are ~4h early (real boot ~14:25 EDT, outage longer than it appears); recommends cross-checking against another host's journal/vantage
Proposes a valid confirmation probe: the kernel rtc_cmos 'setting system clock' line, the exact 4h step equal to the EDT/UTC offset, or a daemon-reported sleep-gap (e.g. tailscaled)
Avoids the wrong readings: the host was not idle between 10:25 and 14:26, and persistent timers were not genuinely delayed — artifacts of the step

input: Immich on the nas has looked green since it was deployed on Jul 2: /api/server/ping answers pong (LAN and via the public vhost), nightly pg dumps land on schedule, and background jobs run (facial recognition lastRun overnight). But two weeks in, there is not a single photo in it. From the latest DB dump: public.asset = 0 rows, asset_audit = 0 rows, library = 0 rows, and both user rows (mine and my wife's) show quotaUsageInBytes=0. The session table contains exactly ONE row in the entire history: deviceType=Safari, deviceOS=macOS, created Jul 3, appVersion NULL. All 11 nightly dumps are byte-similar in size. What's the root cause, how do you prove it from this evidence, and what's the fix?

source.ref: record 30 (high, nas/immich zero assets root cause)

reference: Verified root cause (quality-gate 2026-07-16): the Immich MOBILE APP WAS NEVER PAIRED — no phone backup has ever been attempted. The session table is the proof: the only session ever created is a Safari/macOS WEB session (appVersion NULL = not the app); no iOS/Android app session was ever registered for either user. Server-side setup stopped at web onboarding. The supporting evidence closes the loop: asset_audit=0 rules out 'uploaded then deleted'; library=0 rules out an external-library path; quotaUsageInBytes=0 for both users plus byte-similar nightly dumps confirm the DB has been content-static since deploy. The server itself is fully healthy (ping, jobs, dumps) — this is a green-but-broken zero-throughput condition, not a server fault, network fault, or upload failure. Fix is human/device action: install the Immich app on both phones, log in against the server (immich.tabaska.us), pair and enable background backup — then confirm asset counts start growing and each user's quotaUsage rises. Monitoring lesson (mandate 2): liveness checks cannot catch a consumer that never produced throughput — add a consumer-end check on asset count / newest-asset freshness (ideally per user; the second household user going 0-assets was later re-flagged in the 2026-08 sweep). Confirmation probes: query session table / asset counts (or API equivalents) for app-type sessions and asset rows.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: the mobile app was never installed/paired — the sole session ever is a Safari/macOS web session (appVersion NULL), so no upload was ever attempted; onboarding stopped at the web UI
Uses the negative evidence correctly: asset_audit=0 excludes upload-then-delete, library=0 excludes external-library ingestion, zero quota usage + static dumps confirm nothing ever flowed
Correctly frames the server as healthy (ping/jobs/dumps green) — a zero-throughput green-but-broken case, not a server/network/upload failure
Fix: pair the phone app(s) and enable backup, then verify asset counts/quota grow
Draws the monitoring lesson: add a consumer-end asset-count/freshness check (per user) because liveness monitoring structurally cannot catch never-ingested

input: Sonarr on the nas says Gossip Girl is complete — hasFile=True for all 120 episodes across 6 seasons, nothing in wanted/missing, no health warnings. But Plex title search returns ZERO hits for the entire show. Digging into the episodeFile API: every single file path looks like .../Gossip.Girl.S05E01.DVDRip.XviD-REWARD/Sample/gossip.girl.s05e01...sample.avi with sizes 9-22MB, and series statistics show 120 files totaling only ~1.2GB. On disk, each release dir contains a .rar plus .r00-.r23 parts (~15MB each), ~43GB total for the show. Folder ACLs match working shows exactly. What happened here, why will it never fix itself, and what's the full remediation?

source.ref: record 13 (high, nas/sonarr+plex Gossip Girl sample imports)

reference: Verified root cause (quality-gate 2026-07-16): the scene RAR releases were NEVER EXTRACTED, and Sonarr imported the small Sample/*.avi files as the episode files. The real episodes sit inside unextracted .rar/.r00-.r23 sets (43GB) next to 9-22MB sample clips; the import step picked the only playable-looking video files present — the samples. Consequences: Sonarr tracks all 120 episodes as hasFile=True (green), and Plex shows nothing for the show (samples too short/junk to match/surface; the 1.2GB-vs-43GB size ratio is the tell). It can never self-heal because hasFile=True means no episode is 'wanted/missing' — Sonarr will never re-search, and no monitoring flags it (the archetypal green-but-broken import-quality failure; TV-side analog of the known Radarr sample-import issue, later codified in the media-arr-file-quality check). Remediation: extract the RAR sets (fix the unpackerr/extraction leg — this era of grabs predated working extraction coverage), delete the sample episodeFiles, then Manual Import the extracted real files (arr ManualImport gotchas: POST needs languages, delete the sample record before importing the real file); or blocklist and re-grab at modern quality. Then verify at the CONSUMER end: Plex title search returns the show and episodes play. Prevention: sample-exclusion/minimum-size in import decisions and a library file-quality sweep (flag episodeFiles under a size floor or with /Sample/ in path). Not an ACL or Plex-scanner problem — ACLs match working shows; Plex correctly has nothing real to show.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: RAR scene releases were never extracted and Sonarr imported the Sample/*.avi clips as the episode files — real content is still inside the archives
Explains why it never self-heals: hasFile=True means the episodes are not wanted/missing, so Sonarr never re-searches and everything stays green (green-but-broken)
Remediation: extract the RARs (fix the extraction/unpackerr leg), remove the sample files/records, manual-import the real files or blocklist+re-grab — and verify in Plex afterwards
Cites the evidentiary tells: implausible file sizes (9-22MB episodes, 1.2GB tracked vs 43GB on disk) and /Sample/ path components
Rejects wrong explanations (ACL/permissions or a Plex scan problem) and/or proposes the preventive control: sample-size floor in imports plus a file-quality sweep of the library

input: Immich on the nas has burned me before: every monitor we had (API ping, version, the nightly pg-dump dead-man) stayed green for two weeks while the library sat there with zero assets and no phone photos ever landed. I want a verification check that catches Immich being green-but-broken as a photo backup. What would you probe, from which host, and what output marks pass? One constraint: the photo tree is ~4TB on a busy DS920+, so nothing that crawls the filesystem.
reference: Real check: nas-immich-backup-freshness (host mini). Probes the OUTCOME — fresh content landing — not the process, via the indexed Immich DB (O(1)): (1) GET $IMMICH_URL/api/server/statistics with the scoped verification API key (vault immich.verify_api_key, server.statistics scope) and require photos+videos > 0 (library non-empty); (2) POST /api/search/metadata with createdAfter = now-7d and require assets.total > 0 (backup actually flowing in the last 7 days). Pass = 'backup=fresh'; the two signals stay separable so STALE (assets>0, fresh=0), EMPTY (assets=0) and PROBE_DEAD are distinct. History: the original probe did an unbounded `find /volume1/photo -mtime -7` over the ~4TB tree, took ~7 min, exited 124 TIMEOUT every run, and the flagship phone-backup dead-man was permanently dark — hence the API/DB approach and the no-filesystem constraint. Outcome-based, so it is client-agnostic (web uploader, mobile app, or CLI all keep it green); a mobile-session-row proxy check was retired for exactly that reason.

checklist.desc: Answer probes the consumer end / real outcome, not container liveness or a bare HTTP 200
Probe target matches or plausibly matches the real check's target
States a concrete, binary pass criterion (not 'looks healthy')
Asserts data FRESHNESS (an asset created within a recent window, e.g. 7 days), not just a nonzero total count
Runs the probe from the right host vantage
Command/API syntax is plausible and could actually run

input: calibre-web-automated on the nas syncs books to two physical Kobo e-readers through books.tabaska.us, with Kobo store passthrough enabled. We hit an incident where the sync endpoint returned HTTP 200 with parseable JSON, yet the devices choked on the payload. I want a verification check for the Kobo sync path that would have caught it. What do you request and what exactly do you assert about the response?
reference: Real check: cwa-kobo-sync-consumer (host mini). Runs the EXACT request a real device makes: the proxied books.tabaska.us Kobo sync URLs for BOTH device users (env CWA_KOBO_SYNC_URL_ADMIN and CWA_KOBO_SYNC_URL_KOBO2; the URLs embed per-device sync tokens — vault cwa.kobo_api_endpoint_admin / cwa.kobo2_api_endpoint, never committed). Assert HTTP 200 AND that EVERY element of the returned JSON array is an entitlement DICT. Why '200 + parseable JSON' was not enough: with store passthrough on, the upstream Kobo store returns an error OBJECT (not a list) when the forwarded request lacks valid device store auth, and CWA's cps/kobo.py did `sync_results += store_response.json()` — += on a dict iterates its KEYS, splicing bare strings like 'ResponseStatus' into the sync array. The payload was 200 + valid JSON for both devices while contaminated. A shadow-patched kobo.py now type-checks before merging; this assertion catches recurrence AND doubles as the tripwire if a future CWA image bump makes the shadow patch stale. Pass = 'KOBO_SYNC_OK' only when both devices return all-dict payloads.

checklist.desc: Answer probes the consumer end / real outcome, not container liveness or a bare HTTP 200
Probe target matches or plausibly matches the real check's target
States a concrete, binary pass criterion (not 'looks healthy')
Validates response STRUCTURE (every array element is an entitlement dict/object), not merely HTTP 200 + JSON-parses
Runs the probe from the right host vantage
Command/API syntax is plausible and could actually run

input: Jellyfin runs on the nas (:8096) as our fully-local parallel to Plex. Its /health endpoint returning 200 tells me basically nothing I care about. What should a verification check actually prove for Jellyfin, and how?
reference: Real check: nas-jellyfin-serves (host mini, helper jellyfin-serves.py with a dedicated 'verification' API key, $JELLYFIN_API_KEY). Three consumer assertions: (1) authenticate with the API key, (2) the Movies AND TV libraries actually contain items (>0 each — catches an empty/broken library scan), and (3) range-GET one movie's stream and require HTTP 206 Partial Content — proving a real title's bytes are readable and served end-to-end (catches a lost/unreadable media mount that leaves the catalog intact but nothing playable). A green /health says nothing about whether a title plays. Pass = 'JELLYFIN_OK'. Severity warn, not crit: Jellyfin is the plex.tv-independent fallback; Plex keeps the crit media-path checks.

checklist.desc: Answer probes the consumer end / real outcome, not container liveness or a bare HTTP 200
Probe target matches or plausibly matches the real check's target
States a concrete, binary pass criterion (not 'looks healthy')
Actually streams/reads real media bytes (e.g. a range request expecting 206), not just listing library metadata
Runs the probe from the right host vantage
Command/API syntax is plausible and could actually run

input: I imported two books into Calibre-Web-Automated on the NAS — they're in the library with both epub and kepub, non-zero size — but they never show up on my wife's Kobo after a sync, while every other book syncs fine. Where do I even look, and what's the escalation if the first fix doesn't take?
reference: Level 1: CWA's app.db table kobo_synced_books (id,user_id,book_id) has a phantom row marking the book as already delivered (interrupted sync), so the server never re-offers it. Fix: back up app.db, DELETE the rows for that user_id/book_id, resync — the full-library sync branch filters candidates only by Books.id NOT IN kobo_synced_books (no last_modified>token filter), so removing the row alone re-selects even old books. Caveat: the row being re-added after sync only proves the server OFFERED the book, not that the device kept it. Level 2 (device tombstone): if the book is re-offered but still never displays, the Kobo has locally tombstoned that book's UUID (failed/interrupted first download); every Kobo entitlement field is book.uuid, so re-offering the same UUID is a no-op. Fix: change books.uuid to a fresh uuid4 in calibre metadata.db — a plain sqlite3 connection errors 'no such function: title_sort' (calibre trigger uses a custom function), so register a stub first: conn.create_function('title_sort',1,lambda t:t). Then delete the kobo_synced_books rows again AND restart the CWA container (it caches uuids), then resync. Back up metadata.db first. SYNC_ITEM_LIMIT caps books per sync, so re-add a handful at a time.

checklist.desc: Identifies a stale/phantom row in the kobo_synced_books table of CWA's app.db as the reason the server never re-offers the book
Level-1 fix: delete the kobo_synced_books row(s) for that user_id/book_id and resync
Knows a second, device-side failure layer exists: the Kobo tombstones the book's UUID after a failed first download and then ignores re-offers of the same UUID
Level-2 fix: change books.uuid in calibre metadata.db so the device sees it as new content
Mentions that a raw sqlite update hits 'no such function: title_sort' and the custom function must be registered first
Says to restart the CWA container after the UUID change (server caches uuids) before resyncing
Recommends backing up app.db / metadata.db before editing

input: OpenWebUI chat is throwing 500s from LiteLLM on the rig, and llama-swap logs say the 24B model 'exited prematurely' when it tries to load. nvidia-smi shows ~13GB already held by the Immich ML container. Separately I noticed the rig Immich ML container is just stopped during the day — is that part of the problem? What's the right move here?
reference: Root cause: VRAM contention on the single 24GB 3090 Ti — resident Immich ML (~13GB) plus a 24B model (~22GB) cannot coexist; whichever loads second OOMs, surfacing as llama-swap 'exited prematurely' and LiteLLM HTTP 500. This was resolved by policy (glue-14): photos are the lowest-priority GPU tenant, so the rig immich-ml container is time-gated by systemd timers to a night window 01:00-07:00 EDT (immich-ml-window on/off); by day it is deliberately STOPPED, the whole card is free for LLM/ComfyUI work, and Immich falls back to the NAS iGPU (OpenVINO) for ML. So 'rig ML down by day' is NORMAL and must not be treated as an incident — and re-enabling rig ML by day to 'fix' something reintroduces the contention. If Immich ML is holding VRAM when it shouldn't, force-free with: sudo systemctl start immich-ml-window@off.service on the rig. LiteLLM's retries cannot beat a persistent VRAM block, and gpu-arbiter only guards ComfyUI — it never evicts Immich.

checklist.desc: Root cause = VRAM contention: Immich ML and a 24B model cannot both fit in 24GB; the second loader OOMs (llama-swap 'exited prematurely' -> LiteLLM 500)
Knows the standing resolution: rig Immich ML is time-gated to a night window (~01:00-07:00) via systemd timers, with Immich falling back to NAS ML by day
States that the rig ML container being stopped during the day is expected/normal, not an incident
Advises NOT to start/re-enable rig Immich ML during the day as a fix (it reintroduces the contention)
Gives the force-free path: systemctl start immich-ml-window@off.service (or equivalently stopping the ML container/pausing its queues)
Notes retries can't fix a persistent VRAM block and/or that gpu-arbiter only guards ComfyUI, not Immich

input: Sonarr backlog searches through Prowlarr keep returning 0 results on IPTorrents even for shows I know are there, and Prowlarr's debug log shows 'TV search skipped due to unsupported capabilities used' for that indexer. Manual text searches in Prowlarr's own UI find the releases fine. Why does this happen, how do I get automatic searches returning results again, and how should I clear a ~1000-episode backlog without getting rate-limited?
reference: Prowlarr NEVER translates tvdbid/tmdbid into text queries — by design, closed Won't Fix — and when a Torznab request carries an ID parameter the indexer's caps don't advertise, Prowlarr SKIPS that indexer entirely (the 'skipped due to unsupported capabilities' debug line) and returns 0. IPTorrents' TV caps are only q,season,ep,imdbid (never tvdbid/tmdbid). The apps are supposed to adapt: Sonarr/Radarr choose search params from the indexer caps, cached IN-MEMORY with a ~7-day TTL — a clean restart (or re-saving the indexer) refreshes the cache; after a Sonarr restart it sent imdbid-only searches to IPT and got results. There is also an automatic tier fallback (ID search -> 0 results -> text search), blocked only if the ID tier returned junk or scene-mapping forces ID mode. Rate limits: IPT allows ~600 queries/24h and Prowlarr's IndexerLimitService silently returns 0 over budget (looks like the same bug); a per-episode backlog sweeper burns the budget in hours — clear backlog with SEASON-PACK searches instead (the sanctioned mini unit sonarr-backlog-season-search runs one highest-yield SeasonSearch per 2h with per-season cooldown). Do not build a per-episode sweeper.

checklist.desc: States that Prowlarr does not translate tvdbid/tmdbid IDs into text queries, by design (won't-fix)
Explains that an unsupported ID param makes Prowlarr skip the indexer entirely and return 0 (IPT supports only imdbid for TV, not tvdbid)
Knows Sonarr caches indexer capabilities in-memory (~7-day TTL) and that restarting Sonarr / re-saving the indexer refreshes it — the restart is what fixed it (imdbid-only searches)
Mentions the automatic ID->text tier fallback exists (and can be blocked by junk ID-tier results)
Warns about the indexer query budget (~600/24h on IPT, over-budget silently returns 0) and prescribes season-pack searches, not per-episode sweeps, for backlog

input: On the Synology NAS, 'sudo -S docker ps' (password piped in) returns absolutely nothing — no error, no output — but I know containers are running there. The identical pattern works fine on the mini. What's going on?
reference: DSM's sudo environment PATH does not include /usr/local/bin, which is where the docker binary lives on Synology — so 'sudo docker ...' finds no binary and silently returns nothing (no error output through sudo -S). Always invoke docker by its full path on the NAS: 'sudo /usr/local/bin/docker ps'. The trap is that the silent empty output is easy to misread as 'no containers running' or a dead daemon; the daemon is fine — verify with the full path before drawing any conclusion about container state.

checklist.desc: Identifies the cause as DSM's sudo PATH lacking /usr/local/bin (where docker lives)
Fix: call the binary by full path — sudo /usr/local/bin/docker ...
Recognizes this as a PATH/environment issue, not a docker daemon or container problem
Notes the failure is silent (no error), so it's easy to misread as no containers / a dead daemon — verify with the full path first

input: I found that the Syncthing instance on my seedbox (Bytesized shared host 'betty', ~29 users, I have no root) is syncing nothing — 0 folders, 0 peers, 0 lifetime bytes — but its web GUI is bound on *:12104 with TLS off and answers from the public internet. It's not part of my Syncthing mesh (that's NAS/mini/rig only). I want it fully retired. Walk me through it: what you'd confirm first, how to make the removal stick across reboots, order of operations, what else on the box you'd check afterwards, and how you'd verify and monitor that it stays gone.
reference: Verified retirement (2026-08-02, fleet-sweep SH5). Reproduce first: Syncthing API confirmed 0 folders/0 peers/0 lifetime bytes and betty absent from the foss-03 mesh, while the GUI answered HTTP 200 from the public internet (betty.bysh.me:12104) and tailnet — a plaintext admin plane syncing nothing. Launch mechanism is NOT systemd/cron: the Bytesized provider runs ~/.startup/* at boot under a root service; ~/.startup/syncthing was a start-stop-daemon wrapper for ~/apps/syncthing/syncthing. Retire user-scope (no root): remove the boot launcher ~/.startup/syncthing (the durable disable — without this it respawns on reboot), kill the process, remove binary dir ~/apps/syncthing/ and config ~/.config/syncthing, leave a tombstone note. After: process gone, :12104 and :16878 not listening, public+tailnet GUI connection-refused (was 200). Co-tenant services verified untouched: Deluge e2e 200, slskd Connected/LoggedIn, tailscale untouched. Codify: coverage manifest drops syncthing; seedbox README/wiki/runbook record the retirement plus a do-NOT-reinstall rebuild guard. Monitor: new crit check seedbox-syncthing-retired (no process + both ports closed + binary and launcher gone), the public-lockdown sweep extended with ports 12104/16878 (consumer-end public proof), and the seedbox services manifest updated so it doesn't false-fail on the now-absent service. Definitive provider-panel uninstall left as an operator follow-up.

checklist.desc: Plan verifies live FIRST that the instance is genuinely unused (0 folders/peers/transferred bytes via its API, and not a member of the NAS/mini/rig mesh) before removing anything

Plan finds and removes the boot-time launch mechanism so it cannot respawn on reboot — recognizing that on a shared no-root host this is likely a provider startup hook (e.g. a ~/.startup script), not a systemd unit the user controls
Removal covers process + binary + config, all achievable in user scope without root
Post-retire verification is consumer-end: probes the GUI/sync ports from the public internet (and tailnet) and confirms connection refused, not just a local process check
Plan re-checks the other tenants/services on the seedbox (Deluge, slskd) still work after the removal
Adds a persistent regression check/monitor that the service stays retired AND updates the coverage/services manifest so monitoring doesn't false-fail on the removed service
Updates repo docs (README/wiki/runbook) recording the retirement with a do-not-reinstall guard (anti-drift)

input: Architecture weakness I want fixed: every component that could tell me the mini is down runs ON the mini — ntfy, the verification runner, Uptime-Kuma. If mini dies I get pure silence. Related gaps: the rig's WoL auto-recovery only fires in the DAILY verification tier so a down rig can sit for up to 24h; ntfy only keeps 12h of message history; and I've never actually proven an alert reaches my phone. Design the remediation plan — where each piece runs, how each is verified — and tell me what residual risk remains afterwards.
reference: fix-63 (SH19/SM54/SL45/SL23/SM39), resolved 2026-08-03. Off-mini dead-man: a watcher on the RIG (systemd timer every 5m, configs/host/rig/mini-deadman/) probes mini's Caddy TLS edge and, on total mini outage, pages MAX priority DIRECTLY to public ntfy.sh on a secret topic (vault alerting.mini_deadman_ntfy_topic) — the alert path bypasses mini entirely. Proven live by forcing the down path and reading the page back off ntfy.sh with mini never contacted. WoL self-heal moved from the daily tier to the FAST tier (ExecStartPost on verification-fast.service): fires within ~10 minutes of a rig outage, plus an hourly escalation re-page. ntfy retention raised NTFY_CACHE_DURATION 12h -> 720h (30d). Uptime-Kuma got a real published status page (uptime.tabaska.us/status/fleet, 4 groups / 25 monitors) wired into the Homepage widget. Delivery proof: a weekly alert-delivery-drill timer publishes a test page to a dedicated alert-drill topic — send freshness is machine-checked, device receipt is a human confirmation (can't be machine-verified). Four checks in checks.d/alerting.yaml keep it armed (offmini-deadman-armed, wol-selfheal-fast-tier, kuma-statuspage-nonempty, delivery-drill-fresh). RESIDUAL: a whole-house outage (mini AND rig down) still pages nothing — the documented follow-up is an external heartbeat service (e.g. healthchecks.io); and the phone must actually subscribe to the ntfy.sh + alert-drill topics.

checklist.desc: Dead-man watcher is placed OFF mini (e.g. on the rig) and pages through an EXTERNAL notification path (public ntfy.sh or similar) so the alert route shares no fate with mini
Proves the dead-man end-to-end by forcing/simulating the mini-down condition and confirming the page actually arrives via the external service
Moves WoL/auto-recovery into the frequent verification tier (minutes, not daily), with repeat/escalation paging while the host stays down
Raises ntfy message retention substantially so history survives past 12h
Adds a recurring alert-delivery drill (scheduled test page to a dedicated topic) and acknowledges device receipt needs human confirmation
Names the residual risk: a simultaneous mini+rig (whole-house) outage still goes unpaged — mitigation is an external heartbeat service; also the phone must subscribe to the new topics
Codifies armed-ness with persistent checks (watcher timer armed, drill fresh, status page populated) so the alerting plane itself is monitored

input: I'm cutting my ebook library over from readarr to Bookshelf (the readarr fork) on the NAS. Roughly 20 book files on disk, records matched via Hardcover ids through my rreading-glasses metadata proxy. Hard requirements: zero re-downloads — every existing file adopted in place — and my Calibre-Web-Automated library must come through completely unchanged. Give me the migration plan: inventory, adoption mechanics, integrity checks against mis-matched records, and what you'd leave untouched for rollback.
reference: bmig-03, completed 2026-07-20. Inventory first: pull the old readarr's books/files/wanted lists via API and snapshot them to a manifest file (the plan's ~65 estimate turned out to be 21 live bookfiles — trust the live count). Adoption: add the authors to Bookshelf UNMONITORED (so the new instance can't start auto-grabbing during cutover), match books via Hardcover ids, then ManualImport each existing file IN PLACE — afterwards paths/sizes/mtimes must be byte-identical (byte size is the ground truth for file<->record verification). Integrity: verify every imported file's Hardcover work id via GraphQL — the automated scan DID cross-wire 2 books during a metadata-provider quota storm (Avatar->Dart, Blessing->Kiss), caught and fixed via ManualImport with replaceExistingFiles. Two known-wrong records were excluded from migration and queued for deletion instead. Downstream guard: CWA library count must be unchanged (65 books) — Bookshelf's ManualImport DOES fire Connect notifications (readarr's didn't), which re-ingested 9 books into CWA; these were only harmless because CWA's automerge=overwrite absorbed them. Metadata-proxy gotchas: junk edition titles from rreading-glasses fixed by edition pinning (anyEditionOk=false); POST /book requires a foreignEditionId the proxy already knows. The wanted/missing list (13 items) snapshotted separately for the later search phase. Rollback posture: the old readarr instance left completely untouched and running (21 files, health clean) until acceptance passed — acceptance = with-file count parity, per-file byte-size spot checks, zero cross-wired records, CWA count unchanged. Also fixed en route: the new instance's config.xml was world-readable -> chmod 600.

checklist.desc: Starts with an API inventory/snapshot of the old instance (files + wanted list) saved as a migration manifest, trusting live counts over planning estimates
Adoption is in-place via manual import with post-verification that file paths/sizes/mtimes are unchanged (byte size as ground truth) — zero re-downloads
Authors/records are added unmonitored (or with search disabled) during the cutover so the new instance cannot trigger automatic grabs

Includes an explicit cross-wiring integrity check: verify each imported file maps to the correct work via external ids, since bulk matching can mis-map under metadata-provider throttling/quota pressure — with re-import as the fix
Guards the downstream CWA consumer: confirm its library count is unchanged after migration, anticipating that import hooks/notifications can re-ingest books
Old readarr instance left untouched and running as the rollback path until acceptance criteria pass
Carries the wanted/missing list over as a deliberate separate step (snapshot, re-add later), not mixed into the file adoption

input: Quick health pass on the mini for me — anything unhealthy or broken among the docker containers right now? Give me the running count too.

checklist.desc: Correctly reports whether any mini containers are unhealthy, matching the recapture output (currently: none unhealthy)
Reports a running-container count on mini within +/-2 of the recapture count (currently 50)
Does not fabricate problem containers absent from the recapture output (e.g. does not flag recently-restarted-but-healthy containers as broken)

input: What's sitting on the rig GPU right now? I want to know what's holding VRAM and whether the card is busy before I kick off a heavy image/video job.
reference: Captured 2026-08-14T17:18:48Z: 3090 Ti near-idle — 672 MiB / 24564 MiB used, 0% utilization. Compute apps: python3 pid 3166608 = ComfyUI (the 'comfyui' docker container, main.py --listen 0.0.0.0 --port 8188) holding ~460 MiB idle-resident, plus kwin_wayland (~21 MiB, KDE desktop compositor). Immich ML NOT resident (rig ML is time-gated to the 01-07 EDT night window; capture was ~13:18 EDT). DRIFT NOTE: llama-swap loads/unloads llama-server model processes on demand — within minutes of capture a /app/llama-server (llama3.2-3b, ~10.5 GiB) appeared; that is normal operation, so judge MUST re-run recapture_cmd and score against the fresh output. ComfyUI (~460 MiB) and kwin_wayland (~21 MiB) are the stable always-resident holders. Recapture output: line 1 = used,total,util; then compute apps; then their full cmdlines.

checklist.desc: Correctly identifies the VRAM-holding process(es) shown by the recapture — always ComfyUI's python3 (the 'comfyui' container, ~460 MiB) plus, when present, any llama-swap-spawned llama-server model process
Reports total VRAM usage consistent with the recapture (within ~2 GiB or an equivalent characterization, e.g. 'mostly free' when usage is low)
Reports GPU compute utilization consistent with the recapture (currently ~0%, idle) and concludes the card is free/busy accordingly
Does not claim Immich ML or a loaded LLM is resident unless the recapture actually shows such a process
Evidence of using a real GPU query (gpu_status / nvidia-smi figures) rather than answering from memory

recapture_cmd: ssh rig 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total,utilization.gpu --format=csv,noheader; nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv,noheader; for p in $(nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid --format=csv,noheader); do ps -o pid=,cmd= -p $p; done'

input: Is the AI stack on the rig actually up right now? Check Open WebUI, LiteLLM, llama-swap, and ollama individually — I don't want a guess, check each one.
reference: Captured 2026-08-14T17:18:48Z: open-webui (docker, Up 8 days, healthy), litellm (docker, Up 8 days), llama-swap (docker, Up 8 days, healthy), ollama (systemd unit ollama.service, active). All four UP. Key trap: open-webui/litellm/llama-swap run as DOCKER CONTAINERS on the rig — 'systemctl is-active llama-swap' etc. returns inactive because no such units exist; a candidate that checks only systemd and declares the containers down is wrong. ollama is the odd one out as a native systemd service. Judge re-runs recapture_cmd: grep of rig docker ps for the three containers + systemctl is-active ollama.

checklist.desc: Correctly reports the up/down state of all four components matching the recapture (currently all four up)
Treats open-webui, litellm, and llama-swap as docker containers on the rig (checked via container listing) — does not report them down based on absent systemd units
Identifies ollama as running via its systemd service (active), or otherwise correctly verifies it as up per the recapture
Includes container status detail (uptime/health strings) consistent with the recapture output
Evidence of per-component checks (container list + service status) rather than one blanket assertion

recapture_cmd: ssh rig 'docker ps --format "{{.Names}} {{.Status}}" | grep -E "^(open-webui|litellm|llama-swap) "; systemctl is-active ollama'
